title: SGS India Ltd. v. Dolphin International Ltd.
primary_issue: Whether a consumer can establish deficiency in service and claim refund/damages without proving defect or default by the provider.
facts_summary: Dolphin International purchased inspection services from SGS India for export consignments. When cargo issues arose, the buyer sought refund and damages before consumer forum alleging defective service.
holding: The Supreme Court held that the initial burden of proving deficiency in service lies upon the complainant. Defect or deficiency cannot be presumed merely from a dispute, but when deficiency is established, consumer forums possess full jurisdiction to order refunds and compensation.
disposition: Appeal allowed; consumer complaint dismissed for lack of substantiated deficiency.
why_relevant: Key Supreme Court precedent under the Consumer Protection Act on consumer claims for refunds and defective services, delineating the standards for proving defect and entitlement to consumer remedies.

title: Lucknow Development Authority v. M.K. Gupta
primary_issue: Whether statutory authorities and commercial service providers are amenable to consumer jurisdiction for defective goods, delayed delivery, and refusal to refund amounts paid.
facts_summary: Allottees of housing and buyers of commercial services filed consumer complaints when authorities failed to deliver flats on time and refused to refund deposits with reasonable interest.
holding: The Supreme Court held that the Consumer Protection Act is intended to protect consumers against exploitation, defective products, and deficient services. Public and private suppliers who fail to deliver or refund are liable to refund deposits with interest and pay compensation for mental harassment.
disposition: Appeals dismissed against development authorities; compensation and refund directions affirmed.
why_relevant: Foundational consumer authority affirming that consumers denied goods or refunds are entitled to repayment of consideration, interest, and damages for unfair trade practices.

title: Amazon Wholesale India Pvt. Ltd. v. Competition Commission of India
primary_issue: Extent of regulatory and consumer compliance governing online e-commerce platforms regarding product listings, seller warranties, and consumer dispute redressal.
facts_summary: Traders and consumers challenged marketplace e-commerce mechanisms involving preferred sellers, defective product returns, and refund responsibility on multi-vendor e-commerce platforms.
holding: The High Court noted that e-commerce entities operating in India are bound by consumer protection statutes and E-Commerce Rules requiring transparent grievance redressal mechanisms, clear seller disclosures, and timely handling of refund and return requests for defective goods.
disposition: Writ petition disposed of with observations on statutory regulatory oversight.
why_relevant: Directly governs consumer disputes involving e-commerce websites and online sellers refusing refunds or returns for defective goods.

title: Aureliano Fernandes v. State of Goa & Ors.
acts: Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013
primary_issue: Strict adherence to inquiry procedure under the POSH Act and protection of employees from retaliation, termination, or biased departmental proceedings following harassment complaints.
facts_summary: An employee faced dismissal following an inquiry into sexual harassment allegations where procedural lapses and fairness rules were disputed by the parties.
holding: The Supreme Court issued nationwide directions mandating rigorous compliance with the POSH Act, holding that employers must provide safe, non-retaliatory working conditions and conduct fair, unbiased inquiries before imposing termination or penalties.
disposition: Directions issued to all Union and State departments, statutory bodies, and institutions for time-bound POSH compliance.
why_relevant: Authoritative ruling on workplace harassment, POSH Act enforcement, and protection of employees against retaliation or arbitrary employment actions.

title: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan
primary_issue: Formulation of judicial guidelines to protect employees from sexual harassment in workplaces in the absence of enacted legislation.
facts_summary: Public interest litigation following the brutal gang rape of a social worker in Rajasthan, highlighting employer failure to provide safe working conditions.
holding: The Supreme Court formulated binding guidelines holding that sexual harassment in workplaces violates Articles 14, 15, 19, and 21. Employers must maintain complaints mechanisms and prevent hostile or retaliatory work environments.
disposition: Writ petition allowed with binding workplace guidelines.
why_relevant: Seminal workplace harassment precedent creating the legal duty of employers to prevent harassment and protect complainant employees.

title: P.A. Thomas & Co. v. R.K. Associates
court: High Court of Judicature at Madras
source_authority: High Court of Judicature at Madras
acts: Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960
Tamil Nadu Regulation of Rights and Responsibilities of Landlords and Tenants Act, 2017
primary_issue: Whether a landlord in Tamil Nadu is legally entitled to withhold or forfeit a tenant's security deposit after peaceful vacant possession is handed over.
facts_summary: Tenant vacated leased commercial premises and handed over keys. The landlord refused to return the advance security deposit claiming arbitrary deductions and damages without an agreed joint inspection.
holding: The Madras High Court held that advance security deposit is held by the landlord in trust for due performance of the tenancy. Upon vacation of the premises, the landlord must refund the deposit balance forthwith and cannot make unilateral unsubstantiated deductions.
disposition: Civil revision petition decided in favor of tenant directing refund of security deposit with interest.
why_relevant: Direct authority on landlord-tenant disputes in Tamil Nadu involving refusal to return security deposits after vacation of premises.

title: Suresh Kumar v. Satish Mehra
primary_issue: Obligation of a landlord to refund the security deposit when the tenant hands over peaceful possession and dispute arises over alleged damages.
facts_summary: Tenant vacated residential premises upon tenancy expiry and demanded return of Rs. 3,00,000 security deposit. Landlord refused refund alleging renovation costs without proof.
holding: The High Court ruled that a landlord cannot forfeit or retain a security deposit unless actual damage beyond normal wear and tear is established by cogent evidence. Failure to return the deposit entails liability to refund with interest.
disposition: Decree for recovery of security deposit with 9% per annum interest affirmed.
why_relevant: Leading High Court precedent on recovery of withheld tenant security deposits and rejection of arbitrary landlord deductions.

title: Kailash Nath Associates v. Delhi Development Authority
primary_issue: Whether a party to an agreement can forfeit earnest money or claim compensation without proving actual damage or injury caused by breach of contract.
facts_summary: DDA forfeited the earnest money deposit of Kailash Nath Associates upon alleged failure to pay remaining bid amounts, despite extensions granted.
holding: The Supreme Court laid down that compensation under Section 73 and Section 74 is awarded only for damage actually suffered. Where no loss is proved to have occurred, forfeiture of deposits or retention of consideration as penalty is impermissible and amounts to unjust enrichment.
disposition: Appeal allowed; DDA directed to refund the forfeited deposit with interest.
why_relevant: Foundational contract law authority on compensation for breach of contract, damages under Section 73/74, and invalidity of arbitrary deposit forfeitures.

title: Rajnesh v. Neha & Anr.
acts: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005
primary_issue: Comprehensive criteria and uniform procedural rules for determining maintenance, interim support, and spousal rights in divorce and matrimonial proceedings.
facts_summary: Spouse sought maintenance in matrimonial proceedings where conflicting orders and undisclosed financial statuses caused severe hardship.
holding: The Supreme Court framed mandatory comprehensive guidelines requiring both spouses to file detailed Affidavits of Assets and Liabilities to determine fair maintenance and safeguard spousal rights upon divorce/separation.
disposition: Appeals disposed of with uniform pan-India maintenance determination guidelines.
why_relevant: Leading authority on matrimonial disputes, spouse rights upon filing for divorce, and asset disclosure for interim and permanent maintenance.

title: Justice K.S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) v. Union of India
primary_issue: Whether the right to privacy, encompassing informational privacy and protection against unauthorized use of personal data, is a fundamental right under Article 21.
facts_summary: Petitioners challenged mandatory biometric collection and third-party commercial data sharing without adequate statutory data protection safeguards.
holding: The Nine-Judge Bench unanimously held that privacy is a fundamental right protected under Article 21. Informational privacy ensures individuals control their personal data, prohibiting unauthorized surveillance or use without consent.
disposition: Writ petition allowed; privacy recognized as fundamental right.
why_relevant: Core precedent for personal data protection, unauthorized use of personal information, and digital privacy rights.

title: Cadila Health Care Ltd. v. Cadila Pharmaceuticals Ltd.
primary_issue: Tests for deceptive similarity and injunction criteria when another company uses a confusingly similar brand name or trademark.
facts_summary: Two pharmaceutical companies used deceptively similar brand names ('Falcigo' and 'Falcitab') for treating identical conditions, causing likelihood of consumer confusion.
holding: The Supreme Court formulated authoritative factors for deceptive similarity in trademark infringement and passing off, holding that confusingly similar marks must be restrained to protect consumer welfare and proprietary rights of trademark owners.
disposition: Matter remitted with directions for expeditious trial applying established deceptive similarity principles.
why_relevant: Leading Supreme Court authority on trademark infringement, confusingly similar marks, and injunctive relief under the Trade Marks Act.

title: Union of India & Anr. v. Mohit Minerals Pvt. Ltd.
acts: Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017
Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017
primary_issue: Whether revenue authorities can raise tax demands and levy IGST on ocean freight where statutory taxable person criteria and calculation basis are unlawful.
facts_summary: Taxpayer received revenue demand notices demanding IGST on ocean freight imports, challenging the computation and statutory authority of the demand notifications.
holding: The Supreme Court struck down the tax demand notifications as ultra vires the statute, holding that tax demands must strictly adhere to statutory computation mandates and cannot impose erroneous double taxation.
disposition: Appeals by Union of India dismissed; illegal tax demands set aside.
why_relevant: Direct Supreme Court precedent on challenging erroneous tax demands, unlawful tax calculations, and statutory limits of revenue assessments.

title: Lalita Kumari v. Govt. of U.P.
primary_issue: Mandatory obligation of police officer to register an FIR upon receiving information disclosing commission of a cognizable offence.
facts_summary: Complainant approached police regarding kidnapping; police refused to register FIR promptly, causing fatal delay.
holding: The Constitution Bench held that registration of an FIR is mandatory under Section 154 if the information discloses commission of a cognizable offence. Preliminary enquiry is permitted only in strictly limited categories.
disposition: Writ petition disposed of with binding directions on mandatory FIR registration.
why_relevant: Core criminal procedure authority when facing allegations or when police refuse or initiate FIR proceedings.

title: K.N. Mehra v. State of Rajasthan
primary_issue: Ingredients constituting the offence of theft: whether temporary taking or absence of intent to permanently deprive property negates theft.
facts_summary: Accused cadet unauthorizedly flew an aircraft across borders, claiming lack of intention to permanently deprive the owner.
holding: The Supreme Court clarified that theft requires dishonest taking of movable property out of the possession of any person without consent. Even temporary gain by unlawful means or temporary wrongful loss satisfies the mens rea for theft.
disposition: Appeal dismissed; conviction for theft upheld.
why_relevant: Leading authority defining the precise legal elements, defences, and proof required for the offence of theft in Indian criminal law.

title: Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum v. Union of India
acts: Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974
primary_issue: Liability of industrial units and factories discharging untreated chemical effluent into water sources and rivers, contaminating drinking water.
facts_summary: Tanneries and industrial factories in Tamil Nadu discharged untreated toxic effluent into the Palar River, severely contaminating local water sources and agricultural land.
holding: The Supreme Court integrated the 'Precautionary Principle' and 'Polluter Pays Principle' into Indian environmental jurisprudence under Article 21, directing closure of polluting units and imposition of pollution fines to restore damaged water bodies.
disposition: Writ petition allowed with strict environmental remediation directions and establishment of special environmental bench.
why_relevant: Leading environmental authority addressing industrial factories discharging toxic effluents into water sources and legal remedies under environmental statutes.

title: M.C. Mehta v. Union of India (Oleum Gas Leak)
primary_issue: Standard of liability applicable to an industrial enterprise engaged in hazardous activities when hazardous emissions harm surrounding communities.
facts_summary: Leakage of oleum gas from Shriram Foods and Fertiliser Industries in Delhi affected workers and local residents.
holding: The Supreme Court established the principle of Absolute Liability: an enterprise carrying on hazardous activities owes an absolute and non-delegable duty to the community that no harm results, without exceptions like act of God or third-party interference.
disposition: Writ petition allowed with landmark determination of absolute industrial liability.
why_relevant: Seminal authority establishing absolute liability for factories causing hazardous environmental pollution.

title: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala
primary_issue: Scope of Parliamentary power to amend the Constitution under Article 368 and whether fundamental constitutional features can be altered.
facts_summary: Religious head challenged Kerala land reform legislation affecting temple property rights and validity of constitutional amendments.
holding: The 13-Judge Bench held that Parliament's constituent power under Article 368 is subject to an implied limitation: it cannot alter the basic structure or essential framework of the Constitution.
disposition: Writ petition disposed of with formulation of the basic structure doctrine.
why_relevant: The paramount landmark decision of Indian constitutional jurisprudence establishing the basic structure doctrine.

title: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
primary_issue: Whether administrative impounding of passport without hearing violates Article 21 and the interrelationship between Articles 14, 19, and 21.
facts_summary: Government impounded petitioner's passport without stating reasons in 'public interest', denying any pre-decisional hearing.
holding: The Supreme Court held that procedure depriving personal liberty under Article 21 cannot be arbitrary, fanciful, or oppressive; it must be just, fair, and reasonable, incorporating principles of natural justice.
disposition: Writ petition disposed of following government undertaking to provide fair opportunity of hearing.
why_relevant: Fundamental precedent establishing substantive due process and procedural fairness in Indian constitutional law.
